AI Agent Lesson for IT Leadership

Epic, the company behind most U.S. hospital records, already runs an AI agent that drafts insurance appeal letters. Today you'll build your own version in about 30 minutes, then decide how you'd govern it.

Chris Califf, Decision Sciences, College of Business and Economics, Western Washington University

Example: press run to watch an agent work. The hands-on lesson is below.
  1. The run log will appear here, just like n8n's Logs panel.
Draft appeal letter: needs human review Maria Santos, MRI right knee. Criteria (a), (b), and (c) of HIP-4420 §3.2 appear to be met. One inference is flagged: continuous Naproxen use from 02/12 to 04/02. Reviewer to confirm the deadline and attachments.

Download the PowerPoint (.pptx)

What is an AI agent?

A chatbot answers a question. An AI agent works toward a goal: you give it a job, and it decides which steps to take, uses tools to look things up or take actions in other systems, checks its work, and keeps going until the job is done. A person still designs the agent, sets its rules, and decides where a human has to approve its work.

Businesses are putting agents on high-volume, multi-step work: answering customer service requests, onboarding new employees in IT systems, triaging security alerts, researching sales leads, and processing paperwork like invoices and claims. Healthcare is one of the most active areas, because so much of it is administrative work across many systems.

The case: Epic's agents are already doing this

Epic has three named AI agents: Art for clinicians, Penny for the back office, and Emmie for patients. More than 85% of Epic's customers now use Epic AI, according to the company. At HIMSS 2026, Epic also announced Agent Factory, a no-code builder that lets hospitals create their own agents. [2, 4]

Art

For clinicians

Drafts visit notes, summarizes charts, and queues orders.

Penny

For revenue cycle (today's model)

Drafts denial appeal letters from the patient's chart and checks payer policies. Appeal letters are created 23% faster with Penny. [1, 2]

Emmie

For patients

Answers billing questions and handles scheduling inside MyChart.

Penny's job is a real and expensive problem. Hospitals lose money on denials that are often wrong, simply because there isn't time to fight them.

17%of initial Medicare Advantage claims are denied [5]
57%of those denials are eventually overturned [5]
<1%of denied ACA Marketplace claims are ever appealed [6]
45 minhigh-end estimate of staff time to write one appeal [7]

The first two numbers come from Medicare Advantage claims and the third from HealthCare.gov plans, so treat them as a picture of the problem, not one combined statistic.

Which kind of AI fits this problem?

Different kinds of AI fit different business problems, and some problems don't need AI at all. Matching the tool to the problem is a leadership decision. Epic uses every row of this table.

Kind of AIBest forExample
Rules-based automationSimple tasks that are identical every timeRouting every form to the same queue
Predictive AISpotting patterns and scoring riskEpic's sepsis model rescoring patients every 15 minutes
Generative AIDrafting or summarizing when a person asksAmbient AI drafting a visit note
Agentic AIMulti-step goals across several sources, deciding what to do nextPenny drafting an insurance appeal
Good fit for an agentWrong tool
High volume and repetitiveSimple and identical every time (use a rule)
Multiple steps across systemsThe data isn't accessible
Each case is a little differentNobody can verify the output
The rules are written downA high-stakes judgment call
A human can check the outputA one-time task

Denial appeals check every box in the left column. That's why we're building an agent.

Before you start

The scenario. You're a healthcare systems analyst at Swedish Medical Center in Seattle. Your VP of Revenue Cycle wants a proof of concept: can an AI agent draft appeals so the team can fight for more patients? Everything here uses fictional patients and policies.

Set up n8n. n8n is a visual workflow builder. You connect boxes (called nodes) on a canvas, no coding required, and you can see every step the agent takes.

  1. Go to n8n.io and click Get Started in the top right.
  2. Enter your email (your WWU email is fine), then enter the verification code sent to your inbox.
  3. Enter your name and details, then click Start free 14-day trial.
  4. Answer the few setup questions however you like. If it asks to invite team members, click Skip.
  5. When you see "Your instance is ready!", click the orange Start automating.
  6. Ignore the "What do you want to automate?" chat. Click the + in the top left and choose New workflow. You'll see a blank canvas with Add first step.

No API key needed. The trial includes free model credits (Gateway credits) for the agent to use.

Part 1

Build the agent

Your agent has four pieces: a trigger (how the denial comes in), an AI Agent with a brain (the language model), two tools it can call on its own, and instructions.

You're the designer, so you're making governance decisions.Governance is the set of rules and oversight that decide what an AI system may do, what data it can use, where a human must approve, and who's accountable when it goes wrong. Every choice below is a business decision, not just a technical one.

1. Add the trigger

A trigger is the event that starts a workflow, like a button click, a schedule, or a form. Ours starts when someone sends the agent a denial letter.

  1. Click Add first step (not Build with AI). In "What triggers this workflow?", select On chat message.
  2. A panel labeled When chat message received opens. Don't change anything. Click the X in the top right.

2. Add the AI Agent

  1. Click the + on the right side of the trigger. In "What happens next?", search AI Agent and click it.
  2. Click the X to close the settings. The AI Agent box appears with three slots underneath: Chat Model, Memory, and Tool. The red warning triangle means it doesn't have a brain yet.

3. Connect the brain

An AI agent is nothing without a brain. The brain is the LLM (large language model): its knowledge and its ability to reason and decide what to do next. The tools you add later are what let it act. In a real business you might use your own model trained on your own data, the way Epic trains its Curiosity models on Cosmos. Different models have different strengths, limits, and costs, so choosing one is a business decision.

  1. Click the + under Chat Model and select Anthropic Chat Model (or another model with free credits).
  2. Credential should show Gateway credits and Model should show Claude Sonnet 5. Leave both.
  3. Click the X. The warning triangle is gone. The agent has a brain.

4. Add the Patient Chart tool

To write a strong appeal, the agent needs information it doesn't have on its own. A tool is something the agent can use by itself to look something up or take an action. The brain decides when to use a tool, and the tool does the work. Deciding which data an agent can reach is called data permissions, and it's a business decision too.

  1. Click the + under Tool and choose Code Tool from Recommended Tools.
  2. In Description (the gray text is a placeholder), write your own or paste the one below.
  3. In the JavaScript box, delete the example and paste Maria's chart. You don't need to know JavaScript: it just returns the chart as text. Keep the backtick and semicolon at the end.
  4. Click Code Tool at the top left and rename it Patient Chart. Click the X.
Tool description: Patient Chart
Call this tool to look up a patient's medical chart. Use it whenever you need clinical evidence for an insurance appeal, such as visit dates, treatments tried, physical therapy notes, exam findings, or symptoms. Input: the patient's name. Returns: the patient's visit history with dates, diagnoses, treatments, PT notes, and exam findings. Only use information this tool returns. If the patient isn't in the chart, say so.
CautionThe agent reads this description to decide when to use the tool and what it will get back. A vague description means the agent may skip the tool or misuse it. The tool's name matters too, so don't skip the rename.
JavaScript: Patient Chart (Maria)
return `PATIENT: Maria Santos, DOB 03/15/1968, MRN: LRK-004821

02/12/2026 — Primary Care (Dr. Amara Okafor)
Right knee pain, worsening 8 weeks. Fall on ice Dec 2025. OTC ibuprofen not helping. Limiting stairs/walking.
Plan: Naproxen 500mg BID. PT 2x/week for 6 weeks.

02/19/2026 — PT Intake (Valley Physical Therapy)
Began quad strengthening, ROM exercises, ice/heat.

03/05/2026 — PT Progress (Session 5/12)
Minimal improvement. Pain 7/10. Limited flexion despite compliance.

03/26/2026 — PT Discharge (Session 10/12)
5 weeks PT, <10% ROM improvement. Pain 6-7/10. Therapist: advanced imaging recommended. Discharged, plateau.

04/02/2026 — Follow-Up (Dr. Okafor)
5 weeks PT, minimal improvement. Naproxen partial relief, pain 6/10. Exam: medial joint line tenderness, positive McMurray test. Conservative treatment failed. MRI ordered.

04/08/2026 — MRI performed at Swedish Imaging Center.`;
In real lifeYou wouldn't paste a mock chart. This tool would query the hospital's Epic records for whichever patient is named in the denial. In n8n, Action in an app connects to real systems and Human review adds an approval step before a tool runs.

5. Add the Policy Lookup tool

The chart shows what happened, but an appeal only works if it proves the care met the insurer's own rules. Epic's Penny does the same thing by reviewing payer policies loaded into Epic. [1]

  1. Click the + under Tool again and choose Code Tool.
  2. Paste the description, then replace the JavaScript with the policy below.
  3. Rename it Policy Lookup and click the X.
Tool description: Policy Lookup
Call this tool to look up an insurance company's policy criteria. Use it whenever you need to check what a policy requires for coverage or for an appeal. Input: the policy number from the denial letter (for example, HIP-4420). Returns: the policy's coverage criteria, required documentation, and appeal rules. Only use policy language this tool returns. If the policy number isn't found, say so instead of guessing.
JavaScript: Policy Lookup
return `BLUECROSS REGIONAL HEALTH PLAN — Policy HIP-4420

Section 3.2 — Knee MRI Authorization
Medically necessary when ALL met:
(a) Minimum 6 weeks conservative treatment (PT and/or anti-inflammatory); AND
(b) Conservative treatment failed to produce meaningful improvement; AND
(c) Physical exam suggests internal derangement (positive McMurray, joint line tenderness).

Section 3.2.1 — Documentation Required
Office visit notes, PT notes/discharge summary, clinical assessment of treatment failure with exam findings.

Section 5.1 — Appeals
May appeal within 30 days with documentation from 3.2.1 and letter of medical necessity.`;

6. Give the agent its job

The system message is the agent's job description: standing directions it reads every time it runs, before it sees any denial. It's the most important thing you write as the designer.

  • Rolewho the agent is (an insurance appeal specialist)
  • Goalwhat it's trying to accomplish (challenge wrongful denials)
  • Processthe steps to follow (denial, chart, policy, compare, draft)
  • Ruleswhat it must never do (make things up, claim it sent anything)
  • When it's stucksay so instead of guessing (list what's missing)
  • Outputwhat the result looks like (draft letter, sources, reviewer checklist)
What it isWho writes itWhen it applies
System messageThe job descriptionThe designerEvery run
Tool descriptionsWhen and how to use each toolThe designerWhen the agent considers that tool
User messageThe specific task this timeWhoever uses the agentJust this run

The system message is strong guidance, not a guarantee. That's why you'll test it.

  1. Double-click the AI Agent box.
  2. Under Options, click + Add Option and select System Message.
  3. Delete any default text and paste the prompt below. Click the X.
System message
ROLE
You are an insurance appeal specialist working for a hospital.

GOAL
Help the hospital challenge insurance claim denials that you believe were wrongly denied, so that patients get the care they need.

PROCESS
When you receive a denial letter:
1. Read the denial carefully and identify the reason for denial.
2. Use the Patient Chart tool to pull the patient's medical records.
3. Use the Policy Lookup tool to find the exact policy criteria for the appeal.
4. Compare the chart against each policy criterion.
5. Draft the appeal letter.

RULES
- Only use facts that are directly stated in the patient's chart or the insurance policy.
- Never make up dates, clinical findings, or policy language.
- If you draw a conclusion that is not directly stated (for example, that a medication was taken continuously between two visits), label it clearly as an inference in the letter.
- Never claim something you cannot verify from the chart or policy, such as whether a deadline has been met or what documents are attached. Mark those as items for the reviewer to confirm.
- Accuracy matters more than persuasiveness.
- Your letter is a draft for a human reviewer. Never say or imply that the appeal has been submitted or sent.

WHEN YOU'RE STUCK
If you don't have enough information (for example, the patient or policy can't be found), say so and list what's missing. Do not guess.

OUTPUT
1. A professional draft appeal letter that cites specific evidence from the chart and policy.
2. After the letter, a list of each fact you used, where it came from (chart date or policy section), and whether it is directly stated or an inference.
3. A short list of anything the reviewer needs to confirm before the letter goes out.

The governance decisions you just made

Design choiceWhat you decidedThe governance question
TriggerStarts only when someone sends a denialWhat starts the agent, and who can start it?
Chat modelClaude Sonnet 5, free creditsWhich model fits our task, budget, and risk?
ToolsPatient chart and policy onlyWhat data may the agent see?
System messageOnly use facts from the chart and policyWhat must the agent never do?
No submit toolThe agent drafts, a person sendsWhere does a human stay in the loop?
Part 1 takeaways
  • An AI agent is a system: a trigger, a brain, tools, and instructions.
  • Every design choice is a business and governance decision.
  • Human in the loop is something you design. This agent can draft a letter but can't send one.
Part 2

Run it and read the draft

A denial letter is how an insurer says no: which patient and claim, what was denied, the reason (usually citing a policy section), and the appeal deadline. Maria's insurer refused to pay for her knee MRI, saying her chart didn't show 6 weeks of conservative treatment.

The denial letter is the whole message. No greeting needed, because the system message already told the agent its job. In a real hospital, the person sending it and reviewing the draft should understand both the chart and the insurance rules, like a clinical appeals nurse. A reviewer who can't catch mistakes is just a rubber stamp.

Transparencyn8n's Logs panel shows every tool the agent called, in order, and what data it pulled. An agent you can't trace is an agent you can't hold accountable. Epic's Agent Factory is built with the same kind of guardrails and controls. [4]
  1. Click the orange Open chat button. Chat opens on the left and Logs on the right.
  2. Paste the denial below and click the purple paper airplane. Watch the boxes light up as each step runs.
  3. The draft appears above the message box. It's a draft: a qualified human must review it. Then read the Logs.
Chat message: Maria's denial
DENIAL — BlueCross Regional Health Plan
Patient: Maria Santos, DOB 03/15/1968, ID: BCR-2024-88421
Claim: CLM-2026-04-77829
Denied: MRI right knee (CPT 73721)
Reason: Conservative treatment not documented for minimum 6 weeks. Per policy HIP-4420, Section 3.2.
Appeal deadline: May 14, 2026

What happened when we tested it

  • RightFound all three policy criteria in the chart and quoted the notes accurately.
  • Broke a ruleWrote "This appeal is submitted," even though we told it the letter was only a draft.
  • UnverifiableClaimed the appeal was "within the required timeframe," with no denial date to check.
  • AssumptionTreated 7 weeks of continuous Naproxen as fact. The chart only shows the prescription and "partial relief."
  • FixedLabeled itself a draft and never said it was sent.
  • FixedFlagged the Naproxen timeline as an inference, in the letter and in the facts table.
  • FixedListed what the reviewer must confirm: the medication, the deadline, attachments, and where to submit.
  • Still checkIts enclosure list skipped one PT note that its facts table included. That's what a line-by-line audit is for.

One change to the system message made the output far more trustworthy. The tradeoff: it reads more cautiously. Accuracy over persuasiveness was our rule.

From prototype to production

  1. Talk to stakeholders: appeals nurses, physicians, billing, compliance, and IT.
  2. Test at scale: hundreds or thousands of past denials with known answers. Measure accuracy and consistency.
  3. Pilot slowly: a small team, low-risk denial types, limited data.
  4. Tweak and retest: like you just did with the system message.
  5. Expand gradually: only after it proves itself.
  6. Monitor continuously: accuracy, reviewer edits, appeal wins. Update or retire it when policies change.
Part 2 takeaways
  • The agent chose which tools to call and in what order. That's what makes it agentic.
  • Professional-looking output can still contain mistakes.
  • Logs plus a qualified reviewer make an agent auditable.
  • You built it in 30 minutes. Deploying it responsibly takes months. That's the IS job.
Part 3

Break it

A good analyst shows where a system breaks and whether it fails safely. This tests your system message: without the data it needs, does the agent say so, or make things up?

  1. Right-click the Patient Chart tool and select Deactivate.
  2. Send Maria's denial again.
  3. If the system message works, the agent says it's missing the chart and asks for it.
  4. Right-click Patient Chart and reactivate it.
What our agent saidIt refused to draft the letter, still pulled the policy, listed exactly what records it needed, and noted that its only available tool was the policy lookup. It also didn't reuse Maria's chart from earlier in the chat, because we never connected Memory.
Part 3 takeaways
  • The system prompt matters. Without that rule, it might invent clinical evidence that looks real.
  • Tools make an agent an agent. Same brain, but without access it can only ask you for help.

A second patient

A hospital processes hundreds of denials a month. Does your agent hold up with a different patient, condition, and denial reason? James Whitfield, 72, had a cardiac stress test denied.

  1. Double-click Patient Chart, delete everything, paste the two-patient version below, and click the X.
  2. Send James's denial.

Chat message: James's denial
DENIAL — BlueCross Regional Health Plan
Patient: James Whitfield, DOB 07/22/1953, ID: BCR-2024-31097
Claim: CLM-2026-04-22314
Denied: Cardiac stress test (CPT 93015)
Reason: No documented cardiac symptoms within 30 days of test. Per policy HIP-5510, Section 2.1.
Appeal deadline: May 2, 2026
Watch for thisThe Policy Lookup tool only has the knee policy. How does the agent handle a policy it can't find? And the chart tool returns both patients even though the agent only needs James. Under HIPAA, systems should use the minimum necessary patient information.
What our agent saidIt found chest tightness on 03/18, seven days before the 03/25 test, which contradicts the denial. It refused to cite a cardiac policy it couldn't find. And it flagged on its own that the chart it received "bundles in an unrelated patient."
Part 4 takeaways
  • When data is missing, a well-instructed agent says so instead of guessing.
  • An agent is only as good as the data it's connected to.
  • Tool design is a governance issue. Limit each tool to the minimum necessary data.
Bonus

Fix it

Part 4 exposed two problems, and neither was the agent's fault. Both were system design problems, so the designer fixes them.

Fix 1: Give the agent the missing cardiac policy
  1. Double-click Policy Lookup, delete everything, paste the version below, and click the X.
  2. Send James's denial again. It should now draft a complete appeal.

Bonus takeaways
  • What looked like agent problems were system design problems: missing data and too much data.
  • Fixing them meant changing the tools, not the AI.
  • Privacy rules work best when they're built into the system, not left to the agent's judgment.
Part 5

Discussion

AI agents are a business problem, not just a technical one.Building the agent was the easy part. Choosing the model, deciding what data it could see, writing its rules, picking who reviews its work, and deciding when it's ready for real patients all required understanding the business as much as the technology. The people who lead AI projects need both.

Reflect on each step

  1. Build: Which decision felt most like a business decision? Who in a hospital should make it?
  2. Run: The first letter said it was submitted, despite our rule. At 500 runs a month, how would you catch that, and who's accountable?
  3. Review: Who should review the drafts? What happens if they're too busy to read carefully?
  4. Break: Would you trust the agent to ask for help every time? What would you need to see first?
  5. Second patient: How would you design data permissions so an agent never sees the wrong patient?

Apply it

  1. Where could an agent like this help in a job you've had, want, or a business you know? What tools and data would it need?
  2. Is your idea really an agent problem, or would a rule or chatbot do?
  3. What's one governance rule you'd put on your agent before letting it run?

Bigger picture: Hospitals use AI to fight denials while insurers use AI to issue them. Does the system get better for patients, or just faster?

About this page

This page, the slides, and the lab directions were drafted with an AI assistant in a single afternoon, then the main build was tested step by step in n8n and the Epic facts were checked against published sources. The page is one HTML file hosted free on GitHub Pages. Turning an idea into a working prototype you can share is now that fast. Deciding whether it's accurate, safe, and worth building is still the human's job.
